title: Sharp asymptotics of the singularity probability of a random Rademacher matrix
statement: Let M_n be the n x n random matrix with i.i.d. Rademacher (uniform on {-1,+1}) entries and p_n the probability that M_n is singular. Conjecture 2.2: p_n = (2 + o(1)) n^2 2^{-n}. (The source derives the matching lower bound from two rows or columns being equal up to sign, and notes that examining dependencies among 3, 4, 5 ... rows would give sharper conjectures with smaller error terms.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Tikhomirov (Ann. Math. 2020) proved the weaker Conjecture 2.1, p_n = (1/2+o(1))^n, as the source itself records. Jain, Sah and Sawhney (GAFA 2021, arXiv 2010.06554) proved the sharp form P(singular) = P(zero row or column) + (1+o(1)) P(two rows or columns equal up to sign) for entries whose law is NOT uniform on its support; the Rademacher law is uniform on {-1,1} and is exactly the case their theorem leaves out. Irmatov's announced proof for the Rademacher case (mentioned in the source's Remark 2.5) is reported by Song (arXiv 2509.06408, 'Singularity of biased discrete random matrices', 2025) to have unresolved issues acknowledged by the author. I found no paper claiming the (2+o(1)) n^2 2^{-n} asymptotic for Rademacher entries. Kept open.

attempt.method: Calibrate the conjecture against the next dependency structures, and state the exact reduction the JSS method leaves for the uniform case.
attempt.result: Lower bound: for a fixed pair of rows the probability that they are equal or opposite is 2 * 2^{-n}, and there are C(n,2) row pairs and C(n,2) column pairs, giving (2+o(1)) n^2 2^{-n} with the pair events essentially disjoint; this is the source's (1). The next structure is a linear relation among three or four rows with coefficients +-1. Three Rademacher rows cannot sum to zero coordinatewise (an odd number of +-1 cannot vanish), so the first correction comes from four rows with r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4 = 0 (up to signs): per coordinate 6 of the 16 sign patterns sum to zero, so the probability is (3/8)^n per 4-tuple, and there are O(n^4) 4-tuples. Since 3/8 < 1/2, this correction is O(n^4 (3/8)^n) = o(n^2 2^{-n}), consistent with the conjecture; the same calculation with k rows gives rate (c_k)^n with c_k = P(a sum of k Rademachers vanishes) which is at most 3/8 for all even k >= 4 and decreasing in k. So the conjecture is exactly the statement that singularity is, to leading order, a two-row or two-column coincidence. The JSS argument reduces this to a sharp inverse Littlewood-Offord statement: the normal vector v of the span of n-1 random rows must satisfy P(X . v = 0) <= (1+o(1)) 2^{-n+1} * (the two-coordinate atom) unless v is supported on two coordinates. For non-uniform laws the atom probability of a single coordinate coincidence is strictly less than the two-coordinate one and the counting closes; for Rademacher entries the single-coordinate and two-coordinate atoms have the same exponential rate 1/2, and that is the degeneracy that leaves the polynomial factor undetermined.
attempt.obstruction: Everything below the exponential rate is lost in Tikhomirov's inversion-of-randomness argument, which discretises to precision e^{-cn}; and the JSS counting of structured normal vectors needs the gap between the exponential rates of one-coordinate and two-coordinate coincidences that the uniform law does not provide. Closing the polynomial factor for Rademacher entries requires a local limit theorem for X . v uniform over normal vectors v with polynomially many exceptions, which no current inverse theorem gives.
attempt.key_identity: P(r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4 = 0 coordinatewise) = (6/16)^n = (3/8)^n, so all higher dependency structures are exponentially negligible relative to the pair term n^2 2^{-n}.
attempt.independent_check: The (3/8)^n count is elementary: the number of sign vectors in {+-1}^4 with zero sum is C(4,2) = 6.

title: Singularity probability of a random symmetric Rademacher matrix is (1/2+o(1))^n
statement: Let M_n^sym be the random symmetric n x n matrix whose entries on and above the diagonal are i.i.d. Rademacher, and let p_n^sym be the probability that it is singular. Conjecture 3.3 (Singularity, symmetric): p_n^sym = (1/2 + o(1))^n.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Campos, Jenssen, Michelen and Sahasrabudhe, 'The singularity probability of a random symmetric matrix is exponentially small' (JAMS 2024, arXiv 2105.11384) prove p_n^sym <= e^{-cn} for an absolute c > 0, improving the exp(-n^{1/2}) bound the source cites. I found no result giving the constant 1/2 in the exponent; the CJMS abstract states an unspecified c. Kept open: the source's conjecture is the sharp base 1/2, and the gap between e^{-cn} and (1/2)^n is exactly what remains.

attempt.method: Compute the first-order lower bound in the symmetric model exactly and locate what the CJMS quadratic inverse Littlewood-Offord machinery loses.
attempt.result: Rows i and j of a symmetric matrix are equal if M_ik = M_jk for the n-2 columns k outside {i,j} (probability 2^{-(n-2)}) and M_ii = M_ji = M_jj, which by symmetry is the single condition M_ii = M_ij = M_jj (probability 1/4): total 2^{-n}. With the sign-flipped version and C(n,2) pairs this gives p_n^sym >= (1+o(1)) n^2 2^{-n}, so the symmetric singularity probability is, to first order, again a two-row coincidence and the conjectured base 1/2 is the natural one; the analogue of Phenomenon I would predict p_n^sym = (1+o(1)) n^2 2^{-n}, a sharper statement than the source makes. In the symmetric model the last row X enters the determinant through a quadratic form Q(X) = sum a_ij X_i X_j plus a constant, so the singularity probability is controlled by the concentration of a Rademacher chaos of order 2 rather than a linear form. The known exponential bound comes from an inverse theorem for quadratic forms that, unlike the linear case, cannot yet identify the extremal structure (a quadratic form concentrating at rate (1/2)^n on its atoms) up to a 1+o(1) factor.
attempt.obstruction: The optimal-constant question needs the rank-one and rank-two structures of the cofactor matrix of M_{n-1}^sym to be shown to be the only ones that make the quadratic form Q attain small-ball probability of exponential order (1/2)^n; the quadratic inverse Littlewood-Offord theorems available (Costello-Tao-Vu, Campos et al.) lose constant factors in the exponent through decoupling, which is where base 1/2 becomes base e^{-c}.
attempt.key_identity: P(row i = row j in M^sym) = 2^{-(n-2)} * P(M_ii = M_ij = M_jj) = 2^{-n}.

title: Sharp exponent of the singularity probability of a random d-regular graph, d fixed
locator: Section 5, open question after Theorem 5.2, PDF p. 8
statement: Let A_{n,d} be the adjacency matrix of the uniformly random simple d-regular graph on n vertices, d >= 3 fixed. Huang proved that P(A_{n,d} is singular) <= n^{-c} with c = min{1/8, (d-2)/(5d-6)}, and noted that the singularity probability is at least n^{-d+2}. The source: 'It is interesting open question to find the sharp value of the exponent.'
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Nguyen and Pan, 'A note on the singularity probability of random directed d-regular graphs' (arXiv 2308.06461, European J. Combin. 2024) improve Huang's bound to n^{-1/3+o(1)} for fixed d, via singularity modulo a prime, a local CLT and a large deviation estimate. The abstract states the bound is for the directed model, with the undirected case handled similarly; neither paper claims the exponent d-2. Kept open: the lower bound n^{-(d-2)} and the upper bound n^{-1/3+o(1)} still differ for every d >= 3.

attempt.method: Identify the structure behind the lower bound and reduce the conjecture to a 'no other local structure' statement; explain why the mod-p method cannot reach it.
attempt.result: The lower bound comes from twins: two non-adjacent vertices u, v with N(u) = N(v). For a fixed pair, in the configuration model the d neighbours of u and of v coincide with probability of order n^{-(d-1)}... more precisely the d half-edges of v must land in the d specific vertices already chosen by u, probability (d!) prod_{i<d} (d-i)/(dn) up to constants = Theta(n^{-d}), and there are C(n,2) pairs, giving expected number Theta(n^{2-d}) of twin pairs; a twin pair gives the kernel vector e_u - e_v. A second-moment computation shows that the number of twin pairs is asymptotically Poisson, so P(twins exist) = (c_d + o(1)) n^{2-d}. The sharp-exponent conjecture implicit in the source is therefore P(singular and no twins) = o(n^{2-d}). For d = 3 the target is n^{-1}. Other local kernel vectors need a set S of vertices and a weight vector w on S, orthogonal to every row: every vertex outside S sees zero weighted sum over its neighbours in S, and every vertex of S sees zero over its neighbours. In a locally tree-like d-regular graph a finite-support kernel vector forces a cycle structure of bounded length containing the support; each such pattern has probability n^{-(number of extra edges forced)} and twins are the pattern with the fewest forced coincidences (d-2 of them beyond the two edges available), so the twin exponent d-2 should be sharp among bounded-size structures. What is missing is the global part: kernel vectors with support of size growing with n. Huang's method works modulo primes p and can only show P(rank drop mod p) <= n^{-c}; the n^{-1/3} of Nguyen-Pan is a limitation of the local CLT over F_p, not of the structure.
attempt.obstruction: Bounding P(singular over Q, no bounded-size structure) by o(n^{2-d}) needs an anti-concentration estimate for the last row of a random regular graph conditioned on the rest, and rows of A_{n,d} are dependent with only d ones, so all Littlewood-Offord tools (which need many independent coordinates) fail; the mod-p route can never see the exponent d-2 because the number of primes used is bounded.
attempt.key_identity: E[number of twin pairs] = C(n,2) * P(N(u)=N(v)) = Theta(n^{2-d}).

title: Non-singularity of the k-core of the giant component of G(n, c/n)
statement: Conjecture 4.7 (k-core). Let c > 1 be a constant and set p = c/n. There is a constant k_0 such that for all k >= k_0 the following holds. With probability 1 - o(1), the adjacency matrix of the k-core of Giant(n, p) is non-singular. (The source defines the k-core as a maximal connected subgraph in which all vertices have degree at least k, and notes the giant component itself is singular because it contains cherries.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Glasgow, Kwan, Sah and Sawhney, 'The exact rank of sparse random graphs' (arXiv 2303.05435) give a combinatorial description of the rank of A(G(n,c/n)) for all constants c not equal to e: the corank equals the number of isolated vertices left by the Karp-Sipser leaf-removal procedure plus a term coming from certain cycles in the Karp-Sipser core. A search-result summary states that with high probability the k-core of G(n,p) is full rank for k >= 3 'in certain regimes'; I did not read the paper to confirm which regimes, nor whether the statement covers the k-core (rather than the Karp-Sipser core) for all c > 1. Kept admitted with this lead: anyone merging this row should read arXiv 2303.05435 for a k-core statement before treating the conjecture as open or closed. Related: Coja-Oghlan, Ergur, Gao, Hetterich, Rolvien on ranks of matrices with prescribed row and column sums, and 'On the rank, kernel, and core of sparse random graphs' (arXiv 2105.11718).

attempt.method: Relate the k-core to the Karp-Sipser core, where rank is now understood, and isolate the step the conjecture needs.
attempt.result: The Karp-Sipser core is obtained by repeatedly deleting a leaf together with its neighbour; a vertex of degree >= k >= 3 in the k-core keeps degree >= 3 inside the k-core and every vertex of the k-core keeps at least k neighbours in it, so no vertex of the k-core is ever a leaf and the k-core is contained in the Karp-Sipser core. Nonsingularity of the Karp-Sipser core, which the Glasgow-Kwan-Sah-Sawhney description reduces to the absence of certain cycles, does not pass to principal submatrices, so the conjecture is not a corollary. What does pass is the local structure: the k-core of G(n, c/n) is, conditionally on its degree sequence, a uniformly random graph with that degree sequence (Luczak; Janson-Luczak), and its degree sequence is asymptotically Poisson(mu) conditioned on being >= k for an explicit mu = mu(c,k). So the conjecture is equivalent to: the adjacency matrix of a random graph with a fixed degree sequence of minimum degree k >= k_0 and bounded tails is nonsingular whp. For regular degree sequences this is Huang's theorem (fixed d >= 3); for the d-regular case the obstruction to singularity was twins with probability n^{2-d}, and in a degree sequence with minimum degree k the analogous twin probability is at most n^{2-k}, which tends to zero for k >= 3. This suggests k_0 = 3 should suffice, with the singularity probability of order n^{2-k} times a constant, and the conjecture reduces to extending Huang's mod-p invertibility argument from d-regular to sequences of bounded, min-degree-k degrees.
attempt.obstruction: Huang's argument uses the exact regularity through the switching method and the local CLT for the number of solutions mod p; a non-regular degree sequence breaks the symmetry the switching count relies on, and the k-core's degree sequence is random with unbounded (though Poisson-tailed) maximum degree. No published nonsingularity result for the configuration model with a non-regular degree sequence was found.
attempt.key_identity: A vertex of the k-core (k >= 3) has at least k neighbours inside the k-core, so the k-core survives Karp-Sipser leaf removal and is a subgraph of the Karp-Sipser core.

title: Size and limiting law of the determinant of a random d-regular graph
statement: Question 6.7. Estimate the determinant of A_{n,d}. Find the limiting law. (Context: for fixed d the matrix A_{n,d} has full rank whp by Huang's theorem, so det A_{n,d} is non-zero; 'Its magnitude, however, is unknown.')
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 for the log-determinant of the adjacency matrix of a random regular graph with fixed degree. The results returned the Kesten-McKay law, the local semicircle law for d >= (log N)^4 (Bauerschmidt-Huang-Knowles-Yau) and functional limit theorems for linear eigenvalue statistics (Dumitriu-Johnson-Pal-Paquette), none of which addresses log|det|. No paper stating a limit law for det A_{n,d} at fixed d was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compute the first-order answer from the Kesten-McKay law and identify what a limit law would need.
attempt.result: log|det A_{n,d}| = sum_i log|lambda_i| is a linear eigenvalue statistic of the unbounded function log|x|. The empirical spectral measure converges to the Kesten-McKay law mu_d with density d sqrt(4(d-1) - x^2) / (2 pi (d^2 - x^2)) on |x| <= 2 sqrt(d-1), and a numerical evaluation of L_d = int log|x| dmu_d gives exp(L_3) = 1.1547 = 2/sqrt(3), exp(L_4) = 1.2990 = 3 sqrt(3)/4, exp(L_5) = 1.4311 = 16/5^{3/2}, exp(L_6) = 1.5528 = 5^{5/2}/36, which fit the closed form exp(L_d) = (d-1)^{(d-1)/2} / d^{(d-2)/2} in all four cases (matched numerically to five digits; not derived). So the first-order prediction is |det A_{n,d}| = exp((1+o(1)) n L_d), i.e. |det A_{n,3}| ~ (2/sqrt(3))^n, provided the eigenvalues nearest zero contribute o(n) to the sum. That proviso is a quantitative invertibility statement: one needs sigma_min(A_{n,d}) >= exp(-o(n)) whp together with a bound on the number of eigenvalues in [-epsilon, epsilon] of order epsilon n (the Kesten-McKay density is bounded near 0, so the local law at mesoscopic scale gives this); Huang's invertibility theorem gives a polynomial lower bound on sigma_min with probability 1 - n^{-c}, which suffices for the first order. For the limiting law: for Wigner matrices log|det| has Gaussian fluctuations with variance (1/2) log n (Tao-Vu), the log n coming from the singularity of log|x| at 0; for fixed d the smooth linear statistics have O(1) variance (Dumitriu-Johnson-Pal-Paquette), so the conjecture this computation suggests is log|det A_{n,d}| - n L_d = Gaussian with variance of order log n, driven entirely by the eigenvalues at scale 1/n around zero.
attempt.obstruction: No local law at the scale of eigenvalue spacing 1/n is known for fixed d (the Bauerschmidt-Huang-Knowles-Yau local law needs d >= (log n)^4 and later work needs d growing), and the fluctuation of log|det| is dominated precisely by that scale.
attempt.key_identity: n^{-1} log|det A_{n,d}| -> int log|x| dmu_d(x), numerically (d-1)^{(d-1)/2} / d^{(d-2)/2} at first order in the exponent.
attempt.independent_check: The closed form was inferred from four numerical values (d = 3,4,5,6) and also matches d = 10 (exp(L_10) = 1.9683 = 9^{4.5}/10^4); it is not proved here.

title: Anti-concentration of the determinant of a random Rademacher matrix at non-zero values
statement: Conjecture 6.8 (Determinant). For any x != 0, P(det M_n = x) <= n^{-(1/2+o(1))n}. (Here M_n is the n x n i.i.d. Rademacher matrix. The source adds that the best current upper bound is exponential [Kahn-Komlos-Szemeredi], and that even the much weaker conjecture that the support of det M_n is super-exponential in size is not known.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 for anti-concentration of det M_n at non-zero values. Found nothing beyond the exponential bounds inherited from the singularity method (KKS; Tikhomirov's method also gives P(det = x) <= (1/2+o(1))^n for any fixed x since it bounds P(X . v = x)). Nguyen and Wood (surjectivity of the n x (n+1) Rademacher matrix, probability prod_{k>=2} zeta(k)^{-1} = 0.4358) is the closest related result. Kept open.

attempt.method: Condition on the first n-1 rows and reduce the conjecture to a local limit theorem for the cofactor vector; use the Nguyen-Wood surjectivity result to see what the gcd of the cofactors does.
attempt.result: Write det M_n = X . v where X is the last row and v is the vector of signed (n-1)-minors of the first n-1 rows. Given v, P(X . v = x) is a Littlewood-Offord probability; if v were a generic integer vector with ||v||_2 = n^{(1/2+o(1))n} (which holds whp by the Tao-Vu determinant theorem applied to the (n-1) x (n-1) minors) and with no additive structure, a local limit theorem would give P(X . v = x | v) = Theta(g / ||v||) for x in the lattice g Z generated by the entries and 0 otherwise, where g = gcd(v_1, ..., v_n). This is the conjectured n^{-(1/2+o(1))n}. Two observations calibrate this. (i) The gcd g is exactly the index of the lattice spanned by the columns of the (n-1) x n matrix in Z^{n-1}, so by Nguyen-Wood g = 1 with probability 0.4358 + o(1) and g >= 2 with probability 0.5642 + o(1); since det M_n is then a multiple of g, P(det M_n = x) is zero on those matrices unless g | x, and g is O(1) in distribution (the Nguyen-Wood limit is a Cohen-Lenstra-type law with finite moments), so the gcd changes the constant but not the exponent, consistent with the conjecture holding for every x != 0. (ii) Turan's identity E det^2 = n! shows det takes values of size ~ sqrt(n!) with all the mass, so a uniform spread over the O(sqrt(n!)) reachable values is exactly n^{-(1/2+o(1))n}: the conjecture says the determinant is as spread out as its second moment allows.
attempt.obstruction: The reduction needs a local limit theorem for X . v uniform over the random cofactor vector v, i.e. that v has no arithmetic structure at scale ||v||, which is a statement about the additive structure of a random lattice's Plucker coordinates; the inverse Littlewood-Offord theory only controls structure up to exponential accuracy (that is where the KKS-type (1-c)^n bound stops), and the small-ball probability of X . v at a point below the scale e^{-cn} is out of reach of every current method.
attempt.key_identity: gcd of the (n-1)-minors of an (n-1) x n integer matrix = index of its column lattice in Z^{n-1}; Nguyen-Wood: this index is 1 with limiting probability prod_{k>=2} zeta(k)^{-1}.

title: Super-exponential smallness of the probability that a random Rademacher permanent vanishes
statement: Conjecture 6.12 (Permanent). The probability that Per M_n = 0 is super exponentially small in n. (M_n is the n x n i.i.d. Rademacher matrix; the source says the current bound is polynomial in n, from Tao-Vu, and that nothing is known about the distribution of |Per M_n|.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Kwan and Sauermann (arXiv 2010.08922) proved |Per M_n^sym| = n^{n/2+o(n)} whp for the SYMMETRIC model (this settles the source's Conjecture 6.11, which is therefore not admitted here). A search-result summary attributes to Kwan and collaborators an exponential anti-concentration bound P(Per M_n = z) <= exp(-c n) for uniformly anti-concentrated entries, which would improve the polynomial bound the source cites but is still exponential, not super-exponential; I did not identify the exact paper. Kept open in the super-exponential form the source states.

attempt.method: Use the divisibility structure of permanents of +-1 matrices to calibrate the conjecture, then compare with the determinant analogue.
attempt.result: The permanent of an n x n +-1 matrix is divisible by a high power of two: the gcd of all permanents of n x n +-1 matrices is 2, 2, 4 for n = 2, 3, 4 (computed exhaustively here), and the classical Krauter-Seifter theorem gives divisibility by 2^{n - log_2 n - O(1)} in general (quoted from memory; the small cases are consistent with 2^{n - ceil(log_2 n)}). So Per M_n lives on the lattice 2^{n - O(log n)} Z while its typical size is n^{(1/2+o(1))n} by Tao-Vu and E Per^2 = n!. If the permanent were spread over its reachable values, the atom at 0 would carry mass about 2^n / n^{n/2} = n^{-(1/2+o(1))n}, which is super-exponentially small: the conjecture is the natural one and the sharp form should read P(Per M_n = 0) = n^{-(1/2+o(1))n}, the same rate as Conjecture 6.8 for the determinant at non-zero x. Note the asymmetry the source points to: for the determinant the atom at 0 is exponentially large ((1/2)^n, from two equal rows) while for the permanent two equal rows force nothing, and indeed the permanent of a +-1 matrix with two equal rows is generically non-zero. The only structure forcing Per = 0 that I can exhibit is a zero submatrix pattern that cannot occur with +-1 entries, so no local structure gives a lower bound and the super-exponential rate is plausible.
attempt.obstruction: The Tao-Vu method expands the permanent along rows and controls it as a martingale; it yields polynomial anti-concentration because each step uses a Littlewood-Offord bound on a linear form whose coefficients (the permanents of minors) are only controlled in size, not in arithmetic structure. A super-exponential bound would need the vector of (n-1)-permanent cofactors to be arithmetically unstructured at scale n^{n/2}, and unlike the determinant case there is no lattice or geometric interpretation to draw on.
attempt.key_identity: Per M_n is divisible by 2^{n - O(log n)} for every +-1 matrix, while E (Per M_n)^2 = n!.
attempt.independent_check: The gcd values 2, 2, 4 for n = 2, 3, 4 were computed by enumerating all 2^{n^2} matrices.

title: Probability that a random symmetric Rademacher matrix has a repeated eigenvalue is (4+o(1))^{-n}
statement: Let s_n be the probability that the spectrum of M_n^sym is not simple. The source observes s_n >= 4^{-n}, the probability that the first three rows are the same (which forces zero to be an eigenvalue of multiplicity at least 2). Conjecture 8.4 (Simplicity): s_n = (4 + o(1))^{-n}. The source adds that the best current upper bound is s_n <= e^{-n^c} for some small c > 0 [Nguyen-Tao-Vu], and that it 'looks plausible that Conjecture 8.4 holds for M_n as well'.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (queries on eigenvalue gaps and simple spectrum of random symmetric Bernoulli matrices). Found the CJMS exponential bound for singularity (2024) and Luh-O'Rourke's exponential bound for the non-symmetric spectrum being non-simple (cited in the source), and an arXiv 2025 paper on eigenvalue gaps of inhomogeneous symmetric discrete matrices (2503.08139) whose abstract I did not verify to give an exponential bound for the gap at fixed n-scale. No paper claiming base 4 was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Enumerate the local structures that force a repeated eigenvalue, to see whether 4 is the right base, and separate the two ways a repeated eigenvalue can arise.
attempt.result: A repeated eigenvalue arises either (a) as a repeated eigenvalue 0, i.e. corank >= 2, or (b) as a repeated non-zero eigenvalue, i.e. a double root of the characteristic polynomial at lambda != 0. For (a) the cheapest structure is three identical (up to sign) rows: rows i, j, k agree in the n-3 outside columns with probability 4^{-(n-3)} and the 3 x 3 diagonal block must be consistent, an O(1) factor, so P(corank >= 2) >= c n^3 4^{-n}; the symmetric analogue of the Kahn-Komlos-Szemeredi corank bound would give P(corank >= 2) <= (1/4 + o(1))^n if the two-dimensional kernel is forced to be a two-row coincidence. For (b), lambda != 0 repeated means M - lambda I has corank >= 2 with lambda algebraic; a repeated non-zero eigenvalue is a single algebraic condition (discriminant of the characteristic polynomial = 0) on the n(n+1)/2 entries, and the discriminant is an integer of size exp(O(n^2 log n)), so a naive equidistribution heuristic puts P(discriminant = 0, lambda != 0) far below any exponential. The conjecture is therefore the statement that (a) dominates and is governed by the three-row coincidence, i.e. s_n = (c + o(1)) n^3 4^{-n} in its sharp form. The reduction that follows: Conjecture 8.4 is implied by (i) P(corank(M^sym) >= 2 and no three rows coincide up to sign) = o(4^{-n}) and (ii) P(some lambda != 0 has multiplicity >= 2) = o(4^{-n}). Part (i) is the corank-2 analogue of Conjecture 3.3; part (ii) has no anti-concentration input at all in current methods, which handle repeated eigenvalues through the resolvent of a rank-one perturbation at every scale of the gap and therefore cannot distinguish an exact coincidence from a gap of size e^{-n^c}.
attempt.obstruction: The Nguyen-Tao-Vu gap method proves gaps >= n^{-C} with probability 1 - e^{-n^c} and is intrinsically limited to stretched-exponential accuracy because it discretises the eigenvector; nothing in the literature bounds the probability of an exact repeated non-zero eigenvalue for discrete matrices below e^{-n^c}.
attempt.key_identity: three rows equal up to sign has probability of order 4^{-n} and forces corank >= 2.

title: No two eigenvalues of a random symmetric Rademacher matrix sum to zero
statement: Conjecture 8.5. With probability 1 - o(1), the singular values of M_n^sym are different. (The source: 'the singular values of a symmetric matrix are the absolute values of its eigenvalues. Thus, this conjecture asserts that there is no two eigenvalues adding up to zero.' The M_n analogue is stated as also open.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (singular values distinct random symmetric Bernoulli matrix; eigenvalues summing to zero). Nothing found addressing lambda_i + lambda_j = 0 for discrete symmetric matrices; the simple-spectrum theorem of Tao-Vu covers lambda_i = lambda_j only. Kept open.

attempt.method: Check whether any local structure forces a pair lambda, -lambda, and reformulate the event algebraically.
attempt.result: Since the spectrum is simple whp (Tao-Vu), the event to rule out is lambda_i = -lambda_j with lambda_i != 0. No sign-symmetry can force this: if D M D = -M for a diagonal sign matrix D then every diagonal entry of M would vanish, impossible for +-1 entries; so unlike the repeated-eigenvalue problem there is no local structure of exponential probability, and the conjectured event should have super-exponentially small probability. Algebraically, lambda_i + lambda_j = 0 for some i != j iff the characteristic polynomial p(x) and p(-x) have a common root, iff Res(p(x), p(-x)) = 0; writing p(x) = E(x^2) + x O(x^2) with E the even and O the odd part, a common non-zero root of p(x), p(-x) is a common root of E and O, so the event is Res(E(y), O(y)) = 0, an integer polynomial identity in the entries. A weaker, provable-looking statement: the number of pairs with |lambda_i + lambda_j| <= delta is O(delta n^2 + o(1)) whp by the semicircle law at mesoscopic scales, so the conjecture is a statement about scale 0 exactly, with no local law able to see it. The natural route is the Nguyen-Tao-Vu gap method applied to the pencil: lambda_i + lambda_j = 0 is an eigenvalue coincidence between M and -M, i.e. a repeated eigenvalue of the block-diagonal matrix diag(M, -M); that matrix has dependent blocks, and the rank-one-perturbation argument of the gap method needs the last row to be independent of the rest, which fails here.
attempt.obstruction: The only technique for exact spectral coincidences in discrete matrices (resolvent plus Littlewood-Offord for the last row) does not apply to coincidences between the spectra of M and -M, because flipping the sign couples the two copies; a resultant-based anti-concentration statement at scale 0 for a polynomial of degree ~n^2 in the entries is far beyond current inverse theorems.
attempt.key_identity: {some lambda_i + lambda_j = 0, lambda_i != 0} = {Res(E, O) = 0} where p(x) = E(x^2) + x O(x^2) is the characteristic polynomial.

title: Probability that a random Rademacher matrix is normal
statement: Let nu_n be the probability that M_n (i.i.d. Rademacher entries) is normal, i.e. M M^T = M^T M. Since symmetric matrices are normal, nu_n >= 2^{-(0.5+o(1)) n^2}. Conjecture 9.2 (Normality): nu_n = 2^{-(0.5+o(1)) n^2}. Known: nu_n <= 2^{-(0.302+o(1)) n^2} (Deneanu-Vu); Ferber, Jain and Zhao noted a lemma there can be improved, changing 0.302 'maybe at the 5th decimal place'.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Deneanu-Vu (arXiv 1711.02842, Adv. Math. 2019) and Ferber-Jain-Zhao (CPC 2022, 'On the number of Hadamard matrices via anti-concentration') are the only results found; the latter's abstract addresses the Deneanu-Vu conjecture only as a motivation. No improvement of the exponent 0.302 toward 0.5 was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Exhibit a second family of normal +-1 matrices of the conjectured size to check the constant, and state the counting problem the conjecture is.
attempt.result: Beyond symmetric matrices, every matrix of the form M = S + D with S skew-symmetric with +-1 off-diagonal entries and D an arbitrary +-1 diagonal is normal: M M^T = (S+D)(-S+D) = -S^2 + D S - S D + D^2 ... this is only normal when D commutes with S, so restrict to D = c I with c = +-1: then M M^T = -S^2 + I = M^T M. That gives 2 * 2^{n(n-1)/2} normal matrices, a second family of size 2^{(0.5+o(1)) n^2} disjoint from the symmetric one; more generally M = S + c I + T with T symmetric is normal iff S commutes with T, and the count of commuting pairs is again 2^{(0.5+o(1)) n^2} unless T is a multiple of I. Permutation-similar images P M P^T of these and the Kronecker-type constructions do not change the exponent. So the conjecture is that the count of normal +-1 matrices is 2^{(0.5+o(1)) n^2}, with several disjoint families attaining the bound. Normality is the system of n(n-1)/2 quadratic equations (M M^T - M^T M)_{ij} = 0, i < j, each equation a sum of 2n products; if each independent-looking equation cost a factor 2^{-1+o(1)}... it does not: each equation, being a sum of 2n +-1 products equal to zero, has probability Theta(n^{-1/2}), and the naive product of n^2/2 such factors gives 2^{-(n^2/4) log_2 n}, far smaller than the truth. So the conjecture asserts massive positive correlation among the normality equations, of exactly the size produced by the symmetric and skew families. The Deneanu-Vu rank-pattern conditioning is a way to count solutions to this quadratic system; improving 0.302 to 0.5 needs a way to see that the quadratic system's solution set is essentially a union of linear subspaces of dimension n^2/2 intersected with the cube.
attempt.obstruction: Counting +-1 solutions of a system of n^2/2 quadratic equations has no general tool: anti-concentration handles one equation at a time and the equations are strongly correlated; the only structural fact available is that normal matrices are unitarily diagonalisable, and unitary conjugation does not interact with the +-1 constraint.
attempt.key_identity: (S + c I)(S + c I)^T = -S^2 + I = (S + c I)^T (S + c I) for skew-symmetric S with +-1 off-diagonal entries and c = +-1.

title: Probability of an integral spectrum for a random symmetric Rademacher matrix
statement: Conjecture 9.4 (Integral spectrum). The probability that M_n^sym has an integral spectrum is 2^{-(.5+o(1)) n^2}. (Known: Ahmadi, Alon, Blake and Shparlinski proved the probability that A(n,1/2) has integral spectrum is at most 2^{-n/400}; Costello and Williams improved this to 2^{-c n^{3/2}}, and their proof can be modified to yield the same for M_n^sym.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (integral spectrum random symmetric matrix probability). Only the Costello-Williams 2^{-c n^{3/2}} bound cited in the source surfaced; no improvement found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Derive the Costello-Williams-type bound from the semicircle law by pigeonhole, then show the conjecture is implied by a strong form of the source's fingerprint conjecture through a count of possible spectra.
attempt.result: (1) Lower bound: the all-ones matrix J has spectrum {n, 0, ..., 0}, and so does every D J D with D a diagonal +-1 matrix (a similarity); this gives at least 2^{n-1} symmetric +-1 matrices with integral spectrum, so the probability is at least 2^{-n(n+1)/2 + n - 1}, consistent with exponent 1/2. (2) Pigeonhole: tr(M^2) = n^2 exactly, so integer eigenvalues satisfy sum lambda_i^2 = n^2; by the semicircle law all but o(n) eigenvalues lie in [-3 sqrt n, 3 sqrt n], which contains at most 6 sqrt(n) + 1 integers, so some integer lambda has multiplicity >= c sqrt(n), i.e. corank(M - lambda I) >= c sqrt(n). A symmetric corank-k bound of the form P(corank(M - lambda I) >= k) <= 2^{-c k n} (the symmetric analogue of Theorem 4.1 of the source, which Campos et al. type arguments give with some c) then yields the probability bound 2^{-c n^{3/2}} after a union over the O(n) values of lambda: this is exactly the shape of the Costello-Williams bound, and it explains why this route stops at n^{3/2}: the pigeonhole multiplicity is only sqrt(n), and any argument through multiplicities of single eigenvalues cannot exceed exponent 3/2. (3) A different reduction: the number of multisets of n integers with sum of squares n^2 is at most the number of partitions of n^2 into at most n squares, which is exp(O(n)) (each such multiset is determined by the counts m_j of eigenvalues equal to +-j for j <= n, with sum_j j^2 m_j = n^2, a partition of n^2 into squares, and the number of partitions of N into squares is exp(O(N^{1/3})); allowing signs multiplies by at most 2^{O(n)}). Hence there are at most 2^{O(n)} possible integral spectra. If no spectrum is shared by more than 2^{o(n^2)} symmetric +-1 matrices (a quantitative form of the source's Conjecture 11.2 for M_n^sym), then the number of symmetric +-1 matrices with integral spectrum is at most 2^{O(n)} 2^{o(n^2)} = 2^{o(n^2)} and Conjecture 9.4 follows. So Conjecture 9.4 is implied by a strong fingerprint conjecture, and the true difficulty is bounding the size of a cospectral class.
attempt.obstruction: Bounding the number of symmetric +-1 matrices sharing a given characteristic polynomial by 2^{o(n^2)} is open (Godsil-McKay switching shows classes can be non-trivial, but only for matrices with rare structure), and the single-eigenvalue multiplicity route is capped at exponent 3/2 by the semicircle pigeonhole.
attempt.key_identity: sum lambda_i^2 = tr(M^2) = n^2 for every symmetric +-1 matrix, so an integral spectrum is a partition of n^2 into n squares (with signs), of which there are only 2^{O(n)}.
attempt.independent_check: The partition count uses the standard bound: the number of partitions of N into squares is exp(Theta(N^{1/3})), so with N = n^2 it is exp(Theta(n^{2/3})) before signs, even smaller than the 2^{O(n)} claimed.

title: Probability that all eigenvalues of a random Rademacher matrix are Gaussian integers
locator: Conjecture 9.5 (Gaussian integral spectrum), Section 9, PDF p. 15
statement: Conjecture 9.5 (Gaussian integral spectrum). The probability that all eigenvalues of M_n are gaussian integers is 2^{-(1+o(1)) n^2}. (M_n is the non-symmetric i.i.d. Rademacher matrix; the source states this as the M_n analogue of Conjecture 9.4.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (Gaussian integer spectrum random +-1 matrix). Nothing found beyond the source. Kept open.

attempt.method: Repeat the spectrum-counting reduction of the symmetric case and check the exponent 1 against explicit families.
attempt.result: The conjecture says that the number of n x n +-1 matrices with all eigenvalues in Z[i] is 2^{o(n^2)}. Lower bound: every rank-one +-1 matrix u v^T (2^{2n-1} of them) has spectrum {u . v, 0, ..., 0} with u . v an integer, and more generally any matrix similar over Z to a triangular integer matrix; these give 2^{Theta(n)} examples, consistent with the conjectured 2^{o(n^2)}. Counting spectra: the eigenvalues satisfy sum |lambda_i|^2 <= ||M||_F^2 = n^2 (Schur's inequality, with equality iff M is normal), so a Gaussian-integer spectrum is a multiset of n Gaussian integers with sum of norms at most n^2; the number of such multisets is at most exp(O(n)) (partitions of an integer <= n^2 into at most n parts that are norms of Gaussian integers, times the choice of the Gaussian integer of each norm, at most 2^{O(n)} in total). Hence, as in the symmetric case, the conjecture is implied by the statement that no characteristic polynomial is shared by more than 2^{o(n^2)} +-1 matrices, a quantitative form of the source's fingerprint Conjecture 11.2. Note the exponent: since 2^{n^2} matrices in total and only 2^{O(n)} admissible spectra, the conjecture is equivalent to a uniform-in-spectrum cospectral-class bound of 2^{o(n^2)}, and the trivial bound on a cospectral class (all matrices with a given characteristic polynomial) is 2^{n^2}. Nothing below that is known for non-symmetric +-1 matrices.
attempt.obstruction: No bound on the size of a cospectral class of +-1 matrices is available; the semicircle/circular-law pigeonhole that gives 2^{-c n^{3/2}} in the symmetric case fails here because non-real eigenvalues of a non-normal matrix are not constrained by a trace identity beyond Schur's inequality, and the multiplicity of an eigenvalue no longer equals the corank of M - lambda I for non-diagonalisable matrices.
attempt.key_identity: sum |lambda_i|^2 <= ||M||_F^2 = n^2 (Schur), so there are only 2^{O(n)} candidate Gaussian-integer spectra.

title: Irreducibility of the characteristic polynomial of a random Rademacher matrix
statement: Conjecture 11.1 (Irreducibility). With probability 1 - o(1), the characteristic polynomial of M_n is irreducible. (M_n: i.i.d. Rademacher n x n. The source attributes the conjecture to a 2009 conversation with P. M. Wood and, independently, to Babai in the 1970s.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Eberhard, 'The characteristic polynomial of a random matrix' (Combinatorica 2022, arXiv 2008.01223): conditionally on the extended Riemann hypothesis, the characteristic polynomial of the random +-1 matrix is irreducible whp with Galois group containing A_n; unconditionally the same holds if the entry distribution is uniform modulo a product of four distinct primes, which the Rademacher law is not. Ferber, Jain, Sah and Sawhney (Math. Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc. 2023) prove the symmetric analogue, also under ERH. So the conjecture as stated (unconditional, Rademacher entries) is open; it is settled under ERH. Admitted on that basis, with the conditional result recorded.

attempt.method: Record the exact reason the conditional proof needs ERH and what an unconditional proof for +-1 entries would have to supply.
attempt.result: Eberhard's argument reduces irreducibility to the factorisation statistics of the characteristic polynomial modulo many primes p: if phi mod p has the cycle type of a random polynomial over F_p for enough primes, then phi has no factorisation over Z and its Galois group is large by Chebotarev-type arguments. For this one needs the distribution of M_n mod p to look uniform on M_n(F_p) for primes p up to a polynomial in n; a +-1 matrix mod p is very far from uniform for any fixed p, and equidistribution mod p of the characteristic polynomial is proved only for p large compared with n or through a sieve whose error terms are controlled by ERH. The unconditional route in the same paper uses primes where the entry law itself is uniform mod p, which is unavailable for +-1 entries. A calibration of what is at stake: reducibility with a linear factor x - a, a in {0, +-1}, has probability (1/2+o(1))^n each (det M_n = 0 by Tikhomirov; M_n -+ I singular by the Jain-Sah-Sawhney theorem for non-uniform shifted entries), so the probability of reducibility is at least exponentially small, and the conjecture is a statement about non-linear factors, which have no local-structure lower bound at all. The natural unconditional target: show that for a positive proportion of primes p in [n^{A}, n^{B}] the reduction of det(x I - M_n) mod p is equidistributed over polynomials of degree n over F_p up to a factor 1 + o(1); Nguyen-Wood proved exactly this for the constant coefficient (det M_n mod p) and its joint law over several primes, so the reduction is to extend Nguyen-Wood from the determinant to all coefficients jointly.
attempt.obstruction: Joint equidistribution mod p of all n coefficients of the characteristic polynomial (equivalently of the conjugacy class of M_n in GL_n(F_p)) is not known for +-1 matrices; Nguyen-Wood's method (a moment computation for the number of surjections onto finite abelian groups) handles the cokernel, hence the determinant, but not the full rational canonical form.
attempt.key_identity: reducibility with a linear factor has probability >= (1/2+o(1))^n, from det(M_n) = 0 or det(M_n -+ I) = 0.

title: Almost all Rademacher matrices are determined by their spectrum (fingerprint conjecture)
statement: Conjecture 11.2 (Finger Print). A +-1 matrix is determined by its spectrum if no other +-1 matrices (not counting trivial permutations) have the same spectrum. Then almost all +-1 matrices are determined by their spectrum. (The source raises the same question for M_n^sym or G(n,1/2), noting that non-isomorphic cospectral graphs exist but 'should form a negligible part of the set of all graphs'.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (cospectral random matrices, almost all graphs determined by spectrum). The only related published statement I know is Haemers' conjecture that almost all graphs are determined by their spectrum, which is open; numerical evidence (Haemers-Spence, Brouwer-Spence enumerations up to 12 vertices) shows the fraction of graphs with a cospectral mate decreasing after n = 10 but no proof exists. Nothing addressing the +-1 matrix version was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Rewrite the conjecture as a second-moment statement about the characteristic polynomial and compare with the joint anti-concentration that would prove it.
attempt.result: Let N(p) be the number of +-1 matrices (modulo the trivial symmetries) with characteristic polynomial p. The conjecture says sum_p N(p) 1[N(p) >= 2] = o(2^{n^2}), which follows from sum_p N(p)^2 = (1+o(1)) sum_p N(p) = (1+o(1)) 2^{n^2}, i.e. from P(M and M' have the same characteristic polynomial) = (1+o(1)) 2^{-n^2} for two independent copies (after quotienting the trivial group of size n! 2^{2n} = 2^{O(n log n)}). Since the coefficients c_k of the characteristic polynomial are Rademacher chaoses of degree k with c_k of size about C(n,k) n^{k/2}, the number of achievable polynomials is at most prod_k (2 C(n,k) n^{k/2} + 1) = 2^{(1/4 + o(1)) n^2 log_2 n}, which exceeds 2^{n^2}, so there is no counting obstruction to the conjecture and a heuristic of independent coefficients predicts P(same polynomial) = 2^{-(1/4+o(1)) n^2 log_2 n}, far below 2^{-n^2}. The obstacle is that the only coefficient with a proven anti-concentration bound is the determinant, and only to accuracy (1/2+o(1))^n (Tikhomirov) with the conjectured n^{-(1/2+o(1))n} (Conjecture 6.8 of the same source) still open; the second-moment route needs P(c_k(M) = c_k(M') for all k) <= 2^{-(1+epsilon) n^2}, which requires anti-concentration of the whole coefficient vector at a scale 2^{-n^2}, incomparably finer than anything known. For the symmetric case the known cospectral constructions (Godsil-McKay switching, Schwenk trees) require a vertex subset inducing a regular subgraph with every outside vertex adjacent to 0, half or all of it; for G(n,1/2) the expected number of such subsets of size k is at most C(n,k) (3 * 2^{-k})^{n-k} 2^{-Theta(k^2)}... small for all k >= 3, so GM-switching applies to a vanishing fraction of graphs, consistent with the conjecture but not touching other mechanisms.
attempt.obstruction: No tool controls the joint distribution of all coefficients of a random characteristic polynomial at exponential-in-n^2 accuracy; and there is no structural classification of cospectral pairs beyond the known switching constructions.
attempt.key_identity: Conjecture 11.2 follows from P(charpoly(M) = charpoly(M')) = (1+o(1)) 2^{-n^2} for independent copies M, M'.

title: Order sqrt(n) real eigenvalues for a random Rademacher matrix
locator: Conjecture 11.3 (Real Eigenvalues) and Problem 11.4 (Two real roots), Section 11, PDF p. 17
statement: Conjecture 11.3 (Real Eigenvalues). M_n has, with high probability, Theta(sqrt n) real eigenvalues. The source records that Edelman, Kostlan and Shub computed the expected number of real eigenvalues for a Gaussian matrix (of order sqrt n), that Tao and Vu proved the same formula asymptotically for certain random matrices with entries in {0, +-1}, but 'we do not know anything about M_n'; and it states as a first step Problem 11.4 (Two real roots): Prove that M_n has, with high probability, at least 2 real eigenvalues.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Found universality results for the number of real eigenvalues under moment-matching hypotheses (Tao-Vu, 'Random matrices: universality of local spectral statistics of non-Hermitian matrices', which needs the entry law to match the Gaussian to third or fourth moment, which the Rademacher law does not: E xi^4 = 1 versus 3) and physics-literature universality claims (Kanzieper et al. 2016), plus the 2024 bulk universality for complex eigenvalues of real i.i.d. matrices (arXiv 2402.10197) whose abstract concerns the complex bulk, not the real axis. No rigorous result for Rademacher entries was found. Kept open; the two numbered items are recorded as one row because 11.4 is the source's stated first step toward 11.3.

attempt.method: Separate the upper bound, which follows from the local circular law, from the lower bound, which is the whole content, and state what Problem 11.4 needs.
attempt.result: Parity: complex eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs, so the number R_n of real eigenvalues is congruent to n mod 2; for odd n there is at least one real eigenvalue and Problem 11.4 for odd n is the statement that there are at least three. Upper bound: the local circular law (Bourgade-Yau-Yin; Tao-Vu), valid for Rademacher entries, says the number of eigenvalues of M_n / sqrt(n) in any disc of radius r >= n^{-1/2+epsilon} is (1 + o(1)) n r^2 uniformly, so the strip of width n^{-1/2+epsilon} around the real axis inside the unit disc, covered by O(n^{1/2-epsilon}) such discs, contains at most n^{1/2+2 epsilon} eigenvalues, hence R_n <= n^{1/2+o(1)} whp; the upper half of Theta(sqrt n) is therefore essentially known. Lower bound: the Gaussian computation E R_n = sqrt(2n/pi) (1+o(1)) comes from the Kac-Rice formula for the real eigenvalue density rho_n(x) = E |det(M - x I)| ... (Edelman-Kostlan-Shub), and for discrete entries the same formula holds as an identity E R_n = int E[|p'(x)| ... ] only after conditioning that no eigenvalue is exactly real by structure; the difficulty is that for Rademacher entries the density of real eigenvalues near a point x has no closed form and the four moment theorem, which transfers Gaussian local statistics to matching ensembles, cannot be applied because the Rademacher fourth moment is 1. For Problem 11.4 a direct route: for even n, R_n >= 2 iff the characteristic polynomial p(x) = det(x I - M) has a real root, which holds whenever p changes sign on R; p(x) -> +infinity at +-infinity (even degree), so it suffices to find x with p(x) < 0, e.g. to show P(det(x I - M_n) < 0 for some x) -> 1; at x = 0 this is P(det(-M_n) < 0) = P(det M_n < 0 ... ) for even n equals P(det M_n < 0) = 1/2 - o(1) by the sign symmetry (flip one row), which gives R_n >= 2 with probability at least 1/2 - o(1) but not whp. Improving to whp needs the sign of det(x I - M) at several well-separated x to behave like independent fair coins, a joint anti-concentration/decorrelation statement for det(x I - M) over x, which is a special case of the local statistics near the real axis that is open.
attempt.obstruction: Every available universality technique for non-Hermitian local statistics (four moment theorem, Green function comparison) needs the entries to match the Gaussian to at least the third moment, and Rademacher entries fail at the fourth; the Kac-Rice route needs the conditional density of a real eigenvalue, which has no expression for discrete entries.
attempt.key_identity: For even n, P(det M_n < 0) = 1/2 - P(det M_n = 0)/2, so M_n has a real eigenvalue with probability at least 1/2 - o(1).
attempt.independent_check: Sign symmetry: flipping the sign of the first row negates the determinant and preserves the law.

title: Rank resilience of a random Rademacher matrix is (1/2+o(1))n
statement: Given a +-1 square matrix M, let Res(M) be the minimum number of entries one needs to switch (from 1 to -1 and vice versa) in order to make M singular. It is easy to show that Res(M_n) is, with high probability, at most (1/2 + o(1)) n. Conjecture 11.5 (Rank Resilience). With probability 1 - o(1), Res(M_n) = (1/2 + o(1)) n.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Ferber, Luh and McKinley, 'Resilience of the rank of random matrices' (CPC 2020, arXiv 1910.03619): for an n x m +-1 matrix with m >= n + n^{1-epsilon/6}, after switching any (1-epsilon) m / 2 entries the matrix still has full rank whp, 'an asymptotic solution to a slightly weakened version' of Vu's conjecture. The square case m = n, which is Conjecture 11.5, is not covered. Kept open.

attempt.method: Quantify why the union bound fails in the square case and reformulate the conjecture as a covering statement in Hamming space.
attempt.result: Upper bound (the source's easy direction): the Hamming distance between two random rows is Bin(n,1/2), and the minimum over the C(n,2) pairs is (1/2 - o(1)) n whp, so switching that many entries of one row makes it equal to another and the matrix singular. Lower bound via a union bound: Res(M_n) < k means there is a switching pattern E (a +-1 matrix with k entries equal to -1 in the switched positions) with M_n o E singular, where o is the entrywise product; for a fixed E the matrix M_n o E has the same law as M_n, so P(M_n o E singular) = (1/2+o(1))^n, and the union over the C(n^2, k) patterns gives P(Res < k) <= C(n^2, k) (1/2+o(1))^n, which tends to zero only for k <= c n / log n. So the union bound gives Res(M_n) >= c n / log n and nothing better, a factor log n below the conjecture. Equivalently: singular +-1 matrices number at most (1/2+o(1))^n 2^{n^2}, a Hamming ball of radius (1/2 - epsilon) n in {+-1}^{n x n} has volume (n^2)^{(1/2-epsilon)n} (1+o(1))-ish = n^{(1-2 epsilon + o(1)) n}, and the union of balls around singular matrices has size at most n^{(1+o(1)) n} 2^{-n} 2^{n^2}, larger than the whole cube by the factor n^{(1+o(1))n} 2^{-n}: counting alone cannot prove the conjecture, and any proof must show that the singular matrices within distance (1/2 - epsilon) n of a typical M_n are, essentially, only those obtained by making two rows or columns coincide. The Ferber-Luh-McKinley argument gets around the counting loss by having n^{1-epsilon/6} extra columns, which lets them condition on a large full-rank submatrix; in the square case the last row's Littlewood-Offord bound must be made robust under an adversarial change of (1/2 - epsilon) n of its coordinates, which is false for a fixed row (the adversary can choose the coordinates that matter) and true only on average over the random rows, which is the missing ingredient.
attempt.obstruction: A union bound over switching patterns loses a factor n^{Theta(n)} that the sharp singularity bound cannot absorb; the conjecture needs a structural theorem that the near-singular neighbourhood of a random matrix consists only of two-line coincidences, i.e. an inverse Littlewood-Offord theorem that is stable under adversarial sign changes of a constant fraction of coordinates.
attempt.key_identity: P(Res(M_n) < k) <= C(n^2, k) (1/2+o(1))^n, which is o(1) only for k = O(n / log n).

title: Random Rademacher matrices are stubborn: every diagonal switching stays non-singular
statement: Call a {-1,1} (n by n) matrix M stubborn if all matrices obtained by switching (from 1 to -1 and vice versa) the diagonal entries of M are non-singular (there are 2^n such matrices). Conjecture 11.6 (Local resilience). With probability 1 - o(1), M_n is stubborn.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 ('stubborn' matrix, diagonal switching non-singular). Nothing beyond the source was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Show the conjecture sits exactly at the threshold of the union bound and identify the residual.
attempt.result: For each of the 2^n diagonal sign patterns D, the switched matrix M_n(D) has independent entries, each off-diagonal entry Rademacher and each diagonal entry Rademacher (switching a Rademacher variable leaves it Rademacher), so M_n(D) has exactly the law of M_n and P(M_n(D) singular) = (1/2+o(1))^n by Tikhomirov. The union bound over D gives P(not stubborn) <= 2^n (1/2+o(1))^n = e^{o(n)}, which does not tend to zero: the conjecture is exactly at the union-bound threshold and any proof must use that the 2^n singularity events are far from disjoint. They are indeed strongly correlated: the first-order singular structure, two rows i, j equal up to sign, depends on D only through the two diagonal entries (i,i) and (j,j), so the event that SOME D makes rows i and j coincide up to sign has probability at most 4 * 2^{-(n-2)} (the n-2 outside coordinates must agree up to a global sign, the two diagonal coordinates can be fixed by D), and the union over pairs of rows and pairs of columns gives O(n^2 2^{-n}) = o(1). So the pair structures do not obstruct stubbornness; what remains is P(exists D: M_n(D) singular with no two-line coincidence), and by the Jain-Sah-Sawhney theorem for each fixed D this is o(n^2 2^{-n})... only for non-uniform entry laws; for Rademacher entries the best available bound per D is (1/2+o(1))^n with an unspecified o(1), and 2^n times that is not controlled. Hence: Conjecture 11.6 follows from the Rademacher case of the sharp singularity asymptotic (Conjecture 2.2 of the same source, F0001 here) in the strengthened form P(singular, no two lines coincide up to sign) <= 2^{-(1+c)n} for some c > 0, together with the pair-structure union bound above. The row is therefore a corollary of an exponential improvement over Tikhomirov in the structured-exception count, which is what F0001 asks for.
attempt.obstruction: The per-pattern bound (1/2+o(1))^n is too weak by exactly the factor 2^{o(n)} that the union over 2^n patterns costs; removing it needs the sharp two-line asymptotic for Rademacher entries, which is open (Jain-Sah-Sawhney excludes the uniform-on-support case).
attempt.key_identity: P(not stubborn) <= sum_D P(M_n(D) singular) = 2^n (1/2+o(1))^n = e^{o(n)}: the union bound is exactly critical.
